```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(zurds)
ex <- function(f) system.file("extdata", f, package = "zurds")
```

An `.rds` or `.rda` file is a serialized R object, and R objects can hold
code. `readRDS()` and `load()` rebuild everything in the file: closures,
environments, promises. Since R 4.4.0 a promise at the top level of a file
is refused (CVE-2024-27322), but a promise nested in a list, a closure or
an environment still loads, and runs when used.

zurds reads the file without R's deserializer. This vignette shows how to
look before you load, and what its data-only reader does and does not
promise.

## Look first

`rds_info()` reads only the header. `rds_str()` and `rds_toc()` walk the
whole stream but build nothing: a 2 GB `.rda` costs the time to decompress
it, not the memory to hold it.

```{r}
rds_info(ex("model.rds"))
rds_str(ex("model.rds"))
rds_toc(ex("objects.rda"))
```

## Scan

`rds_scan()` lists everything that can run code (`"executes"`), reach
outside the file (`"reaches_out"`), or needs a package to load
(`"needs_package"`), with where it is:

```{r}
rds_scan(ex("model.rds"))
rds_scan(ex("promise.rds"))
rds_deps(serialize(stats::sd, NULL))
```

A linear model carries its formula's environment: loading it gives you
that environment back. The second file holds a promise whose code would
call `system()`.

## Read data, refuse code

`rds_read_data()` is a reader written in C that builds only `NULL`,
logical, integer, double, complex, character, raw and list vectors, with
their attributes. For a data-only file its result is `identical()` to
`readRDS()`.

```{r}
identical(rds_read_data(ex("iris.rds")), readRDS(ex("iris.rds")))
```

Anything else is an error, with the scan attached:

```{r}
cnd <- tryCatch(rds_read_data(ex("promise.rds")),
                zurds_unsafe_content = function(e) e)
cnd$findings
```

or, with `strict = FALSE`, replaced by `NULL` with a warning:

```{r}
rds_read_data(ex("promise.rds"), strict = FALSE)
```

`rds_extract()` reads one object, list element or column the same way,
and `rds_lazyload_extract()` one object of a lazy-load database.

## What the guarantee covers

`rds_read_data()`:

1. never calls `unserialize()`, `eval()` or any function from the file;
2. builds only the types above, with attributes of those types; a
   `class` attribute is kept, and no method of that class is called while
   building;
3. refuses, or with `strict = FALSE` drops, every other type;
4. checks every length and depth against its limits before allocating.

What it does not cover: once you have the object, your own code may
dispatch on its class to methods you have loaded. A data frame is still a
data frame, and a class name from the file can still select a `print()`
method in your session. That is your code, not the file's.

`rds_scan()` and `rds_is_safe()` are advisory for `readRDS()`: a clean
scan means the file holds no type that runs code as it loads, but
`readRDS()` still creates objects of the file's classes. When you trust a
file's code, `rds_extract(use_r = TRUE)` hands one item, and only that
item, to R's own reader, with its scan attached.
